Durlabh Sunday #01 · History

Rāya Asoko: the only carvings that name Ashoka

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Published 22 November 2026

Ashoka left dozens of inscriptions across the subcontinent, yet almost none of them uses his name, and no likeness of him made in his lifetime is known. The only known carvings that name him, labelled in Brāhmī 'King Asoka' (usually printed rāya asoko), were found on a ruined stupa at Kanaganahalli, near Sannati in Karnataka, during excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India that began in 1994. It shows how Buddhists of the Sātavāhana age remembered him, some three to four centuries after his death.

A king who rarely used his name

Ashoka, the third Maurya emperor, ruled from about 268 to 232 BCE. His edicts on rocks and pillars run from Afghanistan to Karnataka, but in almost all of them he calls himself devānaṃpiya piyadasi: 'Beloved of the Gods', Piyadasi. Soon after James Prinsep deciphered Brāhmī in 1837, scholars linked this Piyadasi with Ashoka through the Sri Lankan chronicles. The stones themselves, though, kept the name back.

That changed in January 1915, when a mining engineer named Beadon found a minor rock edict at Maski, in today's Raichur district of Karnataka. It begins devānaṃpiyasa asokasa, 'of the Beloved of the Gods, Asoka'. Only a handful of Ashoka's own inscriptions use the name at all: versions of his minor rock edicts at Maski, Gujarra (Madhya Pradesh), Nittur and Udegolam (Karnataka).

His face is missing too. Mauryan coins are punch-marked with symbols, not royal portraits, and no statue or painting made in his lifetime survives. So whatever we picture when we say 'Ashoka' comes from later hands.

A collapsed roof in Sannati, 1986

The trail to the portrait begins in a temple. In 1986 the roof of the Kalikamba (Kali) shrine in the Chandralamba temple complex at Sannati, on the Bhima river in Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, collapsed and damaged the image. When the image was moved, the stone pedestal on which it had stood turned out to carry portions of Ashoka's edicts. It had served as a pedestal, unread, for a very long time.

That find turned attention to the surroundings. Nearby, at the village of Kanaganahalli, lay a low mound beside the river.

The great stupa by the Bhima

The Archaeological Survey of India began excavating the Kanaganahalli mound in 1994, under K. P. Poonacha. The mound was a Buddhist stupa, cased in carved limestone slabs. The excavation report, Excavations at Kanaganahalli, was published as Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India no. 106 (imprint 2011).

The site yielded well over a hundred short inscriptions in Brāhmī script, many of them naming donors; Maiko Nakanishi and Oskar von Hinüber edited them in 2014, and the DHARMA project publishes digital editions. Monika Zin's 2018 book analyses the 60 massive slabs that once covered the dome.

The stupa was enlarged and embellished under Sātavāhana rule.

The panel: a king, a queen and a parasol

Among the slabs is a damaged panel showing a royal couple at the centre. The king wears a turban and large earrings, and a parasol, the old sign of sovereignty, is held over him. His queen is beside him, and attendants hold the parasol and fly-whisks (chāmara). Along the border above runs a single line in Brāhmī, usually printed rāya asoko: 'King Ashoka'. The scholarly edition of the inscriptions (DHARMA, after Nakanishi and von Hinüber) reads it rāyā asoko, with a long ā in the second sign.

Panels at Sanchi and Amaravati are often identified as Ashoka, and with good reason, but none of them carries his name. At Kanaganahalli the sculptor removed the doubt, and a second slab on the same stupa carries a similar label. So far, these are the only known carvings of the emperor with an inscription naming him.

A portrait made by people who never saw him

The panel is not a likeness. The historian Nayanjot Lahiri dates it to the 2nd century CE, and scholars generally place the Kanaganahalli reliefs in the early centuries CE: some three to four centuries after Ashoka's death. The people who carved it had never seen him. What they had was memory: Buddhist traditions, later gathered in texts such as the Aśokāvadāna, remembered Ashoka as the model Buddhist king, and Sātavāhana-period donors set him among the kings shown on their great stupa.

That is what makes the panel valuable. It does not tell us what Ashoka looked like. It tells us how he was remembered, and that this memory was alive in northern Karnataka, the same region where his own edicts at Maski, Sannati and elsewhere had been cut into stone centuries earlier.

How to read two words of Brāhmī

Brāhmī is read from left to right. Each consonant sign carries a built-in short 'a'. To give it another vowel, the scribe adds a small stroke to the consonant; a vowel at the start of a word has a letter of its own. So the label is written with five signs. As the scholarly edition reads them: rā (r with the long-ā stroke), yā (y with the long-ā stroke), a (the letter for initial a), so (s with the o-stroke) and ko (k with the o-stroke). Without the stroke on the second sign it would read plain ya, which is the whole difference between rāya and rāyā.

Notice the language, too. Rāya (or rāyā) is a Prakrit word for 'king', related to Sanskrit rājan; asoko is the Prakrit form of Aśoka. Books do not agree on how to print the label (newspapers print rāya, the scholarly edition rāyā, and some textbooks and exam guides print rānyo), which is exactly why epigraphists go back to the stone, or to a good photograph of it, before they quote a single letter.

Seeing it today

Kanaganahalli is a protected site of the Archaeological Survey of India in Chitapur taluk, Kalaburagi district, near Sannati. The Hindu reported in 2024 on years of neglect at the site and on new conservation work. Check access with the ASI's Hampi Circle before you travel.

Read it yourself

If two words of Brāhmī can rewrite how we picture an emperor, the rest of the script is worth an evening. Talaash Heritage's Introduction to Brāhmī script teaches you to read Ashoka's own letters, and our guides to Ashoka and his edicts and the Brāhmī script go further. Questions people ask

Is there any portrait of Ashoka made in his lifetime?

None is known. Mauryan coins carry punch-marked symbols rather than royal faces, and no statue or painting of Ashoka from his own time survives. The Kanaganahalli panel was carved some three to four centuries later.

What does 'Rāya Asoko' mean?

'King Ashoka'. Rāya (read rāyā in the scholarly edition) is a Prakrit word for king (Sanskrit rājan) and asoko is the Prakrit form of Aśoka. It is written in Brāhmī script.

Where is Kanaganahalli?

On the Bhima river near Sannati, in Chitapur taluk of Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, northern Karnataka. It is an Archaeological Survey of India site.

Which of Ashoka's own inscriptions use his name?

Only a few: versions of his minor rock edicts at Maski (found in 1915), Gujarra, Nittur and Udegolam. Elsewhere he calls himself devānaṃpiya piyadasi, 'Beloved of the Gods'.
